text:
Chapter Three


It was Saturday morning, Maggie hadn’t had a drop of coffee yet, and she was walking into work. It was a crime. Dean Clearwater’s email announcing the emergency faculty meeting had arrived late last night while she was well into her second shower, trying to remove the sour odor of sulfur and the sticky slime residue from her skin. Despite her scrubbing, she could still smell the pall on the ends of her hair, and she wondered if she’d ever be free of it.


She was already two minutes late for the meeting, but she stopped in the faculty lounge anyway and was thrilled to hear the coffeepot bubbling, no doubt thanks to Edna. She was Dean Clearwater’s admin, who treated all the faculty and staff like they were her own grandchildren. Unfortunately, barista she was not, and the swampy coffee needed heaps of cream and sugar to be palatable, but Maggie still gulped half of it while she walked to the auditorium.


The meeting was well under way as she slipped in quietly, scanning the audience for Dahlia and finding her resting her head on an open palm, looking as tired as Maggie felt. There was an empty seat beside her holding her bag, and Maggie made her way toward it. An audible groan from the gathered faculty echoed in the chamber, though she missed what exactly had set everyone on edge as she slid into the seat next to her friend. Dahlia greeted her with an eye roll.


Dean Clearwater, a small white man with an impressive, fluffy beard and eyebrows to match, sat on the edge of the auditorium stage, putting him at eye level with the faculty seated in the audience. He cringed against another groan, waving his hands as if he could ward off the incoming barrage of complaints.


“It’s temporary,” the dean reassured, the fluff of his beard twitching. Whatever Dean Clearwater was asking them to live without…well, she’d been working at a small college long enough to know that temporary often became permanent. Often became just the way we do things.


Dean Clearwater continued his plea. “The pall is well contained on the third floor and in the northern stairwell. We don’t expect any additional seepage into Ilex Hall or the wider Hawthorn campus.” His tone was careful as he went on. “However, based on our initial examination of the pall, we expect the team working on its removal will need three to four weeks to complete the task.” Maggie straightened her slouch and sat up, exchanging another look with Dahlia. Murmurs filled the auditorium again.


“Three to four weeks?” Dahlia whispered.


“That’s after graduation!” Maggie whispered back.


Whatever incantation had ignited this pall must have been nasty work, with a tangled mess of calculations and a particularly tricky incantation translation. It was the type of spell that typically needed triple and quadruple checking by other experts. Diadhan, the language of magic, was Maggie’s specialty, and she was often pulled into collaborations with other academics to consult on difficult incantation translations. Sometimes, she was only one of many translators working on a Diadhan spell. She shuddered to think how a spell of this magnitude was set off in the same building as hundreds of students. In Arthur Taliesin’s lab, no less. Was it his spell? Or had one of his students conjured something?


“In times like these,” the dean went on, “we so appreciate that Hawthorn spirit that brings us together. Over the next few days, myself, Dean Bobbin, and other administrators will work together to adjust class schedules in the least disruptive way to find available, empty classrooms. And sharing offices with affected colleagues will, hopefully, be a minor inconvenience for everyone.”


Ah. Maggie now understood the collective groan and whispered conversations. She had expected the need to move classrooms around to accommodate everyone, but she was less than thrilled at the idea of squeezing another professor into her small office for the remainder of the semester. It was in a dank corner of the basement that smelled like a century of dust and mildew. She had livened it up with twinkle lights, shelves stocked with books and tchotchkes, and vintage maps of this world and the Otherworlds, but it was still a dark basement office with a narrow window that let in only a sliver of light during the brightest part of the day.


Meanwhile, the third floor was home to the comparably plush accommodations of the Alchemy and Transmutation Department. It was full of bright offices filled with alchemical contraptions, sturdy mahogany built-ins, and ergonomic chairs that would prevent the dull ache that constantly plagued Maggie’s back. Out their windows were scenic views of the lawn and downtown Galloway to the west and the Wilds buttressing the eastern edge of campus. She’d quickly learned that those kinds of offices were for well-funded departments and splashy magic. For departments that didn’t have to fight for every cent their programs spent, with big budgets that weren’t decimated when a bit of funding got shifted around for something else. Not for Diadhan linguists whose work and instruction were essential, sure, but not the kind of thing that got written up in alumni magazines.


The dean droned on about collaboration and camaraderie, unaware that he was on the verge of losing the audience completely, when Arthur Taliesin walked onto the stage, standing slightly in shadow. The color was back in his cheeks and there wasn’t a hair out of place on his head, but he certainly didn’t look thrilled to be standing up there. His mouth was constructed in a downturn, and his eyebrows were pinched together behind his glasses, now smudge-free. It may have been a Saturday, but Taliesin was dressed like he was going to be giving a lecture later in a button-down and slacks. He cleared his throat lightly to alert Dean Clearwater to his presence, but the dean still startled.


“Oh, Arthur! Thank you for joining us,” Dean Clearwater said, gesturing for Taliesin to take a seat next to him, but Taliesin pretended not to notice and continued to stand. Maggie let out a low scoff and shook her head. Taliesin certainly didn’t seem like the sit-on-the-stage-because-we’re-all-friends-here type.


“I guess Clearwater is still trotting out Taliesin like he’s the department mascot,” Maggie said under her breath so only Dahlia could hear. It had been nearly nine months of Let’s see what Dr. Taliesin thinks of that and Have you asked Dr. Taliesin to weigh in, and Maggie was tired of it. “I would have thought setting loose a pall would put a stop to that, but what do I know.”


“He needs to get the most out of his celebrity hire.”


Onstage, Taliesin cleared his throat again, and his hand was in his pocket, fidgeting slightly. His unease surprised Maggie. She was used to seeing him in meetings where he commanded attention, or even catching glimpses of him in front of his class, where his students watched and participated in his lectures with enviable concentration.


Taliesin had been quite the get for Hawthorn when he joined the faculty in the fall. He was well known, even outside academic circles. First, because of his mother’s fame for her pioneering theoretical work in physical transmutation, but then in his own right. Even at his young age—young for academic success, anyway—he had made a name for himself by building on his mother’s work. He transformed her alchemical theory into practical, world-changing spellcraft. Maggie had several items in her apartment right now that worked the way they did only because of Taliesin’s early research. Hawthorn was an unexpected, and confusing, choice for him. He could have taught at any university he wanted, or he could have gone into lucrative private work that would have paid sums of money Maggie could hardly imagine.


But she had been pleasantly surprised when she first met Taliesin last August. He seemed to care, deeply, about both his research and his students. It was a rare combination, especially in someone who could have easily rested on his laurels. But that was before. Before November, when he’d slashed funding to one of her programs during a budget committee meeting without a thought. Before he was irresponsible enough to set off a pall in his own classroom.


“Thank you for graciously agreeing to share your office space with your Alchemy and Transmutation colleagues,” Taliesin finally said to the crowd, shifting from side to side as he spoke. “This will be an inconvenience for everyone, but we are working day and night to remove the pall and mitigate the effects that are being felt across campus. The safety and comfort of our students is our number one priority.


“Office reassignments will be shared via email on Monday morning, and spare furniture will be brought to the basement, first, and second floors this afternoon in preparation. Please direct any questions about your assigned office mate or the planned removal of the pall to Dean Clearwater or Dean Bobbin.” When he was done, several hands shot up in the air, but Taliesin was already walking off the stage.


“What an ass.” Maggie’s whisper was like a hiss. “He told us nothing.”


“What the hell happened in that lab?” Dahlia asked in disbelief, and Maggie just shook her head.


“And not even a single sorry? I would have settled for an oopsie daisy.” A chuckle behind her reminded Maggie that she should definitely keep her voice down, but she couldn’t stop thinking about Taliesin’s complete disregard for their safety. Whatever had happened in that lab had endangered a building full of students and teachers and would be inconveniencing them all for much longer. And he couldn’t be bothered to say anything about it? No, she sincerely doubted that Arthur Taliesin had ever taken accountability for anything in his miserable life.



—


All Monday morning, Maggie had been meaning to find a moment to check her email to learn who her office mate was going to be, but her classes had kept her very busy. Each one ran long as students had dozens of questions about the pall and what it would mean for the rest of the semester.


During her last class, she did her best to reassure them. The pall’s origins may still be a mystery, but she was, at least, confident in the wards protecting the campus. “The pall is contained. It cannot seep through the rune wards,” she promised. Visible relief cascaded over some of the more nervous students.


“What about fantasmia?” a student named Francis asked. Wraiths, ghouls, and even banshees were common enough that every home was warded against them, but they were sure to become more of a nuisance the longer the pall lasted.


“Palls act as beacons for fantasmia. They are drawn to the power the pall pulls from the underworld,” Maggie explained. “It’s reasonable to expect increased sightings the longer this thing is around, so be smart. Don’t travel alone, especially at night. Wear protective runes. And call the campus wardsmith if you notice anything strange.”


When she finally dismissed the class, she made a beeline for her office to boot up her old computer. The basement was a flurry of activity. Her colleagues were busy rearranging furniture and chatting far too merrily with their new office mates. Maggie sighed with relief when there wasn’t anyone from the third floor waiting outside her office for her to return.


As her computer whirred to life, Dahlia’s high-pitched twinkle of a laugh cut through the din in the hallway. Maggie leaned back in her chair to peek out her door and saw Dahlia struggling to carry a heavy wooden desk along with a young Alchemy and Transmutation Biology professor named Jim. His class was a favorite among students. Of course it was. Who wouldn’t want to learn how magic could be used to transform a butterfly into a songbird? She had shared a wall with Jim’s class last semester, and Maggie had appreciated how courteous he was, always checking in to make sure the days he spent demonstrating transmutation didn’t interrupt her exam sessions.


Maggie spun away from her computer. “Do you need any help?” she called out to Dahlia and Jim.


“Please!” her friend said, straining under the weight of her end of the desk.


Maggie lifted the desk next to Dahlia, catty-corner to Jim. A soft sheen of sweat had formed at Jim’s brow, and his winter-pale skin was ruddy with effort, but he had a good-natured smile on his face.


“Maggie! I haven’t seen you all semester.”


“You’ll be seeing a lot more of me now,” she said as they angled the desk into Dahlia’s office, pivoting until it just fit.


The office was chaotic, and that was putting it kindly. Stacks of file folders propped up stacks of books; the trash can overflowed with discarded papers. Maggie knew from experience that every drawer looked like a kitchen junk drawer, but Dahlia had somehow cataloged their contents and could point you to anything you needed. Dahlia’s walls were plain apart from a giant chalkboard hanging on one wall that was currently covered in her careful runes, and she had managed to clear a single, desk-sized space by the door. Somehow, as they angled the furniture into the office, only a single pile of file folders fell over, spilling papers across ancient linoleum.


Jim stood beside the desk, catching his breath, and surveyed the state of his new office as Dahlia gathered the fallen papers. “It’s okay to be horrified,” Maggie said. “Dahlia and I shared a classroom our first year at Hawthorn, and I swear I found an X-ray of her foot in our desk at the end of the year.”


“I’m sorry…what?”


Dahlia scoffed. “That was four years ago, Magnolia.” Maggie scrunched her nose at her full name as Dahlia went on. “I sprained my ankle on campus, and one of the nursing students graciously offered to make sure I hadn’t broken a bone, I’ll have you know. She gave me the X-ray as a keepsake.”


As Maggie and Dahlia continued to squabble about things that happened years ago, Jim studied the runes on the chalkboard appraisingly. He drew closer to a spot on the chalkboard and interrupted their bickering. “What’s this?”


Maggie leaned over Jim’s new desk to get a closer look and practically screeched. “Gods below, Dahlia, are you for real?”


Jim began to read it out loud. “Tall—at least six one. Has a younger brother. Funny in a self-deprecating way.”


Maggie shushed Jim and looked around like there might be someone listening.


“That’s for inspiration,” Dahlia said, ignoring Maggie’s protestations. “We are trying to find Maggie’s mystery man. We went to the Beltane festival on Brig Beach, and Maggie fell in love.”


“Oh, a mystery!” Jim said with a grin. “Thrilling.”


“First of all, I cannot believe you put this on your office chalkboard. Second of all, I did not fall in love,” Maggie muttered, mimicking Dahlia’s singsong tone.


Dahlia shrugged. “Your exact words were ‘I can’t stop thinking about him…’ ”


Before Dahlia could continue that train of thought, Maggie shot her a glare and then turned back to Jim, who was watching the two of them with a bemused expression. “I heard about the masks at this year’s festival. Did they really work?” he asked.


Maggie nodded. “Tall is the only physical thing I’ve been able to remember about him. I didn’t even get his real name.”


“I mean, it’s not the only physical thing you remember about him.” Dahlia said the words quickly, like she couldn’t quite believe she said them out loud.


Maggie held her palm to her face and shook her head, repeating, “Gods below, Dahlia.” She had no idea that her ears could burn so hot with embarrassment.


Jim sighed. “I can’t believe this was the year I had to staff the campus Beltane fair. I should have let Taliesin cover for me when he offered.” To his credit, Jim changed the subject after that with a small smile in Maggie’s direction, and she decided she liked him even more than she thought. “So, who is the lucky member of our department rooming with you?”


Maggie shrugged and grabbed a tissue to erase Dahlia’s absurd list. “I haven’t had a minute to check my email yet.”


“You’re better than I am. I was refreshing my inbox while I drank my coffee this morning.”


“Me, too. This is such a nightmare,” Dahlia groaned. “No offense, Jim.”


“None taken!” he said cheerfully, hopping up onto his new desk and swinging his feet. “None of us in Alchemy and Transmutation are exactly thrilled either. I just got my house keys back this morning after they were stuck behind the pall all weekend. And my lab supplies.” He grimaced and sighed. “I don’t know how we’re going to finish out the year.”


Dahlia’s eyes brightened, and Maggie knew that look. Jim had said a magical combination of words that sometimes pass between coworkers when you suddenly know the other is ready to dish. “So, what happened anyway?” Dahlia asked, her tone a little bit nonchalant and a little bit conspiratorial.


“Oh, well,” Jim said, as if he were stalling. “You know as much as I do, I suspect.”


“I doubt it. Maggie and I were there, and we’ve heard nothing about what exactly happened to bring down that pall.”


Jim glanced up and down the hallway from his vantage point on the desk and turned back to them. “They’re being very quiet about what actually happened. Dr. Taliesin’s class was the only lab in session at the time.”


“I can’t believe Taliesin allowed a student to do a spell strong enough to cast a pall without any additional staff support or spell guardrails, though,” Maggie said.


Jim raised his eyebrows, leaning in toward them. “What if it wasn’t a student?”


Maggie and Dahlia exchanged a glance. “You’re saying the Arthur Taliesin messed up a spell so badly that a destructive, unmovable pall descended on his classroom and infected the entire building?”


“Maybe,” Jim said, shrugging. Maggie wasn’t sure which possibility was worse.


“I saw him that day,” Maggie admitted to Jim. “We both stopped the pall from coming down to the second floor. He seemed…” Maggie tried to find the right words to describe the frantic, angry way Taliesin had moved. “Flustered. I’ve never seen him like that.”


“ ‘Destructive, unmovable pall’! He must have known how bad it was before anyone else,” Dahlia said. The three professors were quiet for a moment, lost in their own thoughts about whatever must have happened that day.


“What’s he really like anyway?” Maggie asked.


“A hard-ass,” Jim said simply, and Dahlia snorted. Coming from a kind professor like Jim, it meant something. “Look, I don’t have any insider information that it was Dr. Taliesin, but I feel pretty confident that he would never cover for a student.”


“Now that I believe. He’s never been anything but a jerk to me,” Maggie declared, wondering briefly if she should be a little bit more professional. But she just thought about the way he’d dismissed her after they stopped the pall, without so much as a thank-you. About the way he’d never once acknowledged his role in slashing her budget and dismantling one of her programs. About the way he had stood up onstage in front of his colleagues and didn’t offer a single explanation for what had happened. “Rude, inconsiderate,” she went on. “Pompous,” she added, for good measure. “A legacy…”


Maggie heard someone clear their throat behind her, and the color drained from Jim’s face as he jumped down from the desk, looking like one of her students caught cheating on an exam. Dahlia’s mouth was curved in a barely suppressed grin, and Maggie knew, without any doubt, who was behind her. She closed her eyes and muttered a curse under her breath. Of course.

facts.fact: 周六清早紧急教工会：她洗第二遍澡仍去不掉 pall 硫磺味，没喝到咖啡就赴会。
院长宣布 pall 封锁三楼与北梯、清理需三到四周——Dahlia/Maggie 惊呼那过了毕业季。
Maggie 专业=Diadhan（魔法语言），常被拉去会诊咒语翻译；她推断能炸出这种量级 pall 的咒计算必乱。
facts.anchor: Diadhan, the language of magic, was Maggie’s specialty

facts.fact: 办公室重派：她办公室在地下室阴湿角落，三楼炼金系却豪华——资源分层怨气。
facts.anchor: a dank corner of the basement

facts.fact: Taliesin 上台被她讥为「系吉祥物」；九个月来全是「问问 Taliesin 博士」。
facts.anchor: trotting out Taliesin like he’s the department mascot

facts.fact: Taliesin 名望：母亲 Rowena 物理嬗变理论成名，他把它转化为实用咒艺；来 Hawthorn 令人费解。
facts.anchor: pioneering theoretical work in physical transmutation

facts.fact: 他宣布重派周一邮件公布，不顾举手离场；她骂「混蛋，什么都没说」。
facts.anchor: several hands shot up in the air, but Taliesin was already walking off the stage

facts.fact: 周一课上她讲 pall 会吸引 fantasmia，叮嘱结伴/戴护符/找 wardsmith。
facts.anchor: Palls act as beacons for fantasmia

facts.fact: 办公室里她正数落 Taliesin，身后一声清嗓、Jim 脸白——cliffhanger。
facts.anchor: the color drained from Jim’s face
